cards.front: The two facts that drive news feed design
cards.back: Feeds are read far more than written, and follower counts are wildly uneven. Together they create the celebrity problem.

cards.front: Feed load rate for 200M users opening the feed 10 times a day
cards.back: About 23,000 a second on average, around 70,000 at the evening peak.
500 post IDs at about 16 bytes each is 8 KB a user, about 1.6 TB for 200M users. Keep timelines only for recently active users.

cards.front: Why cursors instead of page numbers?
cards.back: New posts arrive while you scroll, so ?page=2 would duplicate or skip posts. A cursor encodes exactly where the last page ended.
Push writes each post ID into every follower's timeline at post time (fast reads, write storms). Pull merges followees' posts at read time (cheap writes, slow reads).
Push for ordinary accounts; accounts above a threshold (about 10,000 followers) are pulled at read time from a heavily cached recent-posts list.

cards.front: Why timelines store post IDs, not bodies
cards.back: An edit or delete changes one row instead of millions of copies; the post vanishes at hydration time.

cards.front: How fan-out stays safe under retries
cards.back: Timelines are sorted sets keyed by post ID, so a retried batch re-adds the same members. Workers batch 1,000 followers and checkpoint.
They are time-sortable, so sorting by ID is sorting by time, the ID can be the timeline score, and no central counter is needed.

cards.front: Why store the follow graph twice?
cards.back: Fan-out asks 'who follows X?' and pull asks 'who does Y follow?'. One table per direction makes each a single partition read.
Gather candidates about 10 ms, hydrate about 20 ms, rank about 50 ms, then return 20 posts with a cursor.

cards.front: What happens when the ranker is slow or down?
cards.back: Serve the chronological timeline. A slightly worse feed beats an error screen.

quiz.q: An account with 50M followers posts, and followers see it minutes late while fan-out workers fall behind for everyone. What is the fix?
choices: Add more Redis nodes
Switch accounts above a follower threshold to pull, merging their recent posts at read time
Pull every account's posts at read time
Increase the timeline length to 5,000
quiz.why: The hybrid caps write storms by skipping the push for celebrities.

quiz.q: After a Redis region failover, the posts store's latency spikes and feeds time out. What is happening?
choices: A thundering herd of cold-timeline pull rebuilds
The ranker fell back to chronological
Kafka mirroring stopped
Snowflake IDs collided
quiz.why: Every user's first load is a cold miss; rebuilds must be rate limited and can serve a partial feed first.

quiz.q: A moderator removes a post. How does it disappear from millions of feeds?
choices: Fan-out workers delete it from every follower's timeline
Timelines are rebuilt for every follower
Its status is set and its post-cache entry purged; hydration drops it
The CDN is purged
quiz.why: Timelines hold IDs only, so filtering at hydration removes it everywhere.

quiz.q: Users scrolling a ranked feed see the same post twice on page 2. What design detail was missed?
choices: Idempotency keys on create
The follow graph stored in both directions
Trimming timelines to 500 entries
Storing the ranked list briefly under a snapshot ID so the next page continues the same order
quiz.why: Re-ranking on every page reshuffles candidates; a snapshot keeps pagination stable.

quiz.q: Small accounts' posts miss the 5-second freshness target whenever a 90,000-follower account posts. What helps most?
choices: Route big fan-out jobs to their own queue partition
Lower the celebrity threshold to 100 followers
Make fan-out synchronous in the post API
Cache post bodies in timelines
quiz.why: Separating queues by size stops big jobs from blocking small ones.

quiz.q: Where should photo bytes go when a user posts an image?
choices: Through the post API into Cassandra
Into the Redis timeline
Into Kafka with the new-post event
Directly to object storage with a pre-signed URL, served via CDN
quiz.why: Media never passes through the feed service.

quiz.q: A user returns after two months and has no cached timeline. What does the feed service do?
choices: Return an empty feed
Fall back to pull for that load, then write the result back to the cache
Wait for fan-out workers to backfill
Show only celebrity posts
quiz.why: Inactive users have no timeline; pull rebuilds it on demand.
